transcript:
Header: 2025-02-14 15:00 UTC | Duration: 52m | Attendees: Alice Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Li (Redwood SE), Katie Morris (AtlasHealth ML Eng), Ravi Patel (AtlasHealth Infra), Sofia Alvarez (AtlasHealth CTO)

Summary: Deep dive on throughput tuning for on-prem cluster. Focus areas: continuous batching, scheduler knobs (max_num_seqs, max_batch_tokens), token limits, KV cache sizing and TTL, quantization tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem constraints.

00:00 - Alice Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining—quick intros, Marcus is our inference SE, he'll take most of the tuning stuff.
02:00 - Marcus Li: hi all, yeah hi, Marcus Li. So maybe to start, can you confirm target throughput and latency SLOs? You mentioned earlier 200 QPS and 50ms p95?
03:10 - Katie Morris: yeah thats roughly right, 200 qps peak for short chat completions, 30-60 token responses mostly, and we'd like p95 < 120ms ideally, p99 < 300ms. Not unrealistic for our use case?
04:05 - Marcus Li: okay that helps. So with on-prem you get a few knobs: continuous batching enabled in the runtime, max_num_seqs which controls how many concurrent sequences we pack, max_batch_tokens which sets a cap so a long sequence doesn't blow up a batch, and token limits per request. Also per-GPU concurrency and scheduler preemption.
06:00 - Ravi Patel: when you say continuous batching, is that like Triton dynamic batching? we run kube with GPU nodes, we want to map this to our scheduler.
07:12 - Marcus Li: similar idea. Continuous batching in our runtime keeps a small "batch assembly" thread active; it aggregates requests on the fly, forming a batch whenever either the batch token cap or max_num_seqs is hit or a latency threshold is met. It's optimized for low tail latency while still improving throughput. It's not exactly Triton but conceptually similar.
09:00 - Alice Chen: a lot of customers see best cost/throughput when max_num_seqs is around 6-12 for 4k context LLMs on A100s, but that varies a lot with token length distribution. For short 30-token outputs, smaller max_num_seqs can reduce latency.
11:00 - Marcus Li: yes, and the scheduler knobs: we usually tune max_batch_tokens (e.g., 4096 or 8192) and max_num_seqs together. Example: if your average request is 50 tokens and you want 200 QPS, you'd calculate expected batch size and set max_batch_tokens to limit wasted compute when a single long request arrives.
13:15 - Katie Morris: what's the effect of setting max_num_seqs too high?
14:30 - Marcus Li: you get higher throughput but higher tail latency. If you set max_num_seqs to 32 you'll sometimes wait longer to fill the batch. Continuous batching helps by having a latency cap—if a request sits for more than e.g., 20ms it will flush.
16:00 - Ravi Patel: that latency cap, is it configurable? how deterministic is it under load?
17:10 - Marcus Li: yes it's configurable (scheduler.max_wait_ms), typically we start at 20ms for low-latency apps, 50-100ms for throughput-optimized workloads. Under sustained high load it becomes less of a limiter because batches fill quickly; under bursty traffic it matters more.
19:00 - Marcus Li: another knob is per_gpu_concurrency which controls how many batched requests we can pipeline on a GPU; for small sequences you can increase it, but memory (KV cache) and CUDA streams become the constraint.
20:05 - Sofia Alvarez: about KV cache — if we're doing multi-turn chat with caching, what do we need to watch for?
21:10 - Marcus Li: KV cache saves past key/values to avoid re-encoding prefixes; it's great to reduce compute for long histories. But memory grows with sequence length and batch size. Two things: TTL or reset policy per-conversation, and max_cached_tokens per-conversation. If you let the cache grow unbounded you'll OOM on the GPU. Also cache hits affect batching because cached sequences may have shorter effective decode time.
23:00 - Katie Morris: we typically keep 2k tokens of history per convo. Is that okay?
24:20 - Marcus Li: 2k is common; on A100 80GB you can handle many concurrent convos, but with big batch sizes it adds up. We recommend setting max_cached_tokens=2048 and evict older context once that threshold is hit; also track cache memory usage in the console.
26:00 - Marcus Li: quantization: for on-prem you mentioned you'd prefer 4-bit quant (q4) to save memory. For throughput the tradeoffs are interesting: q4 reduces memory and increases effective batch capacity, but sometimes increases per-token decode time slightly depending on kernel selection. GPTQ-style quant can give good accuracy but requires careful kernel path; redwood runtime has optimized kernels for q4 and int8 on Ampere and Hopper.
28:10 - Ravi Patel: is there a recommended config for q4 + continuous batching? anything special?
29:20 - Marcus Li: the main thing is to ensure you pick quantization-friendly kernel (we detect this automatically) and set batch_token_alignment — we align to 8/16 tokens for efficient matmul. Also reduce per_gpu_concurrency slightly when using lower-precision kernels if you see peak mem spikes. We'll run a quick benchmark.
31:00 - Alice Chen: for their 200 QPS target with short outputs, our quick estimate is: with q4 on A100 80GB, max_num_seqs 8, max_batch_tokens 4096, scheduler.max_wait_ms 25, per_gpu_concurrency 2 should be a good starting point. Marcus, thoughts?
32:20 - Marcus Li: yup that's a reasonable starting point. We'll want to run an actual 30m benchmark to capture tail behavior and Vary the max_num_seqs between 4/8/12. Also try max_batch_tokens 2048 vs 4096 to see if smaller cap helps p95.
34:00 - Katie Morris: what about token limits per request? we sometimes have 4k context windows. Should we cap input tokens?
35:10 - Marcus Li: yes enforce input_token_limit at the gateway level (e.g., 4096). On the runtime side you also want max_decode_tokens to avoid runaway outputs. For throughput you can set a per-request token cap so a single request can't stall batches. Example: max_input_tokens=4096, max_decode_tokens=512.
37:00 - Ravi Patel: network & VPC stuff — if we run private deployment in our VPC, are there any implications for latency due to control-plane calls?
38:15 - Alice Chen: control plane calls are minimal once model is pinned. Model weights and runtime sit in your VPC/on-prem, so inference path is local. Control plane is used for rollouts, telemetry, and management. For strict air-gapped we have an on-prem package.
40:00 - Marcus Li: for telemetry we offer opt-in log shippers; for strict compliance you can push metrics to Prometheus locally and we can integrate with your SIEM. KMS/HSM integrations supported for key sealing; we'll send the docs.
41:30 - Sofia Alvarez: any gotchas running with Kubernetes scheduler and Redwood runtime?
42:20 - Marcus Li: ensure node labels for GPU types and set resource requests so the runtime can place pods with the expected memory for KV cache. We recommend daemonsets per GPU for predictability, and set pod PDBs if you need high availability. Also be careful with preemption — if the node gets preempted you lose KV cache and that affects latency until warm-up.
44:00 - Katie Morris: you mentioned kernel selection earlier, can you expand?
45:10 - Marcus Li: runtime compiles and picks kernels based on architecture, model dims, and sequence length distribution. For quantized models we prefer our int8/q4 kernels with fused attention if supported. If sequence length is short, some kernels are faster; for long sequences another path wins. We log kernel choices in the console for each model serving instance.
47:00 - Alice Chen: ok to recap: Marcus will provide a recommended knobs matrix (max_num_seqs, max_batch_tokens, scheduler.max_wait_ms, per_gpu_concurrency) plus a benchmark config. We'll run 3 variants and share results. We will also share security and VPC docs.
48:30 - Marcus Li: small note on observability: instrument both request size distribution and inter-arrival times; continuous batching heavily depends on inter-arrival distribution. If arrivals are highly bursty you may want smaller scheduler.max_wait_ms.
50:00 - Ravi Patel: understood. any quick wins we can try today?
50:30 - Marcus Li: yes, turn on continuous batching, set scheduler.max_wait_ms=25, max_num_seqs=8, max_batch_tokens=4096, enable KV cache with max_cached_tokens=2048 and do 10k-sample synthetic load test at your cluster. We'll also provide a JMeter config and benchmark script (link).
51:20 - Alice Chen: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the materials.
52:00 - Meeting end: thanks and bye.

References/links mentioned: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/atlas-throughput (spreadsheet), https://redwood.ai/docs/onprem-vpc (on-prem docs), https://redwood.ai/security/kms (KMS integration), benchmark script: https://storage.redwood.ai/benchmarks/atlas-jmeter.zip
